content.text:
Review of trail 1201 (branch `feat/windows-ps1-autoupdate`, 7 commits on top of `feat/windows-powershell-installer`).

**Verdict: sound design, mergeable after small fixes.** The probe refactor is a real improvement: per-OS files replace the runtime `goos` switch for install detection, the Windows fallback now prints the same install.ps1 one-liners the README documents, and the dead cmd.exe branch of the installer runner is gone with a comment explaining why it must not come back. Unix tests, vet for both GOOS values, and unix lint all pass.

**The one open finding was a false positive, and I dismissed it.** It claimed case divergence from `EvalSymlinks` could break Scoop root matching, but the Windows prefix check lowercases both sides, so no case on either side can fail the match. The mixed-case test already covers this.

Things to fix before merging:

- **Uncommitted work in the tree.** Moving `noInstallRoots` into the unix file is correct (only brew uses it, and it would be an unused symbol on Windows), but it is not committed yet.
- **Misplaced doc comment** in `cmd/entire/cli/versioncheck/versioncheck_windows.go:22`. The paragraph describing `scoopAppName` sits above `scoopConfigPath`, and `scoopAppName` itself has no comment.
- **Windows-only lint failures** (CI lints on Ubuntu only, so these won't block, but they will bite anyone running lint on Windows):

```
versioncheck_windows.go:49:15: G304: Potential file inclusion via variable (gosec)
versioncheck_windows_test.go:154:59: string `scoop update entire/entire` has 6 occurrences (goconst)
```
  The gosec hit is a config-file read from a fixed location and deserves a `//nolint:gosec` with that reason. The test string wants a constant.

Lower priority:

- The `name` field on the probe struct, and the three manager constants that feed it, are set but never read. Either drop them or use them in a log line.
- In `scoopAppName`, the `len(normalized) < len(root)` guard is unreachable after a successful prefix match.
- The trail description still says the auto-install predicate "now always returns true". That function was removed two commits later, so the description should say every path has an update command instead.

Verified against the repo: the two Windows one-liners match the README exactly, and `scripts/install.ps1` accepts `-Channel nightly`. The Scoop config keys `root_path` and `global_path` match Scoop's config.json schema.

The advantage is that only one place decides where the root ends.

With `matches` returning a bool, the probe knew the exec path was under a Scoop root but threw away where. Scoop's command then needed the app-dir segment right after that root, so it re-ran the whole search: read the exec path again, read config.json again, resolve symlinks per root again, and repeat the prefix loop, plus a second hand-rolled `Cut` on the default marker. Two detectors had to agree, and the tests covered the copy rather than the probe.

`locate` returning the remainder gives the command the one fact it needs. Scoop's command becomes "first segment of the remainder equals `cli`", with no second search and no duplicate of the marker logic.

The cost is that brew and mise ignore the remainder, so their command funcs carry an unused parameter. If you would rather keep `matches` as a bool, the alternative is a Scoop-specific `scoopAppName(execPath)` that reruns root detection, which is what was there before. I think one extra ignored argument is cheaper than a second detector.

Only Scoop cares *where* the match ended, because it must read the app directory right after the apps root to tell a pre-rename `cli` install from an `entire` one.

Follow-up to #2152. Depends on #2152 (`feat/windows-powershell-installer`).

Users who installed via `install.ps1` currently get the GitHub releases page when Entire reports an update. This prints the README one-liners instead:

```
irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 -UseBasicParsing | iex
& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 -UseBasicParsing))) -Channel nightly
```

Windows still never auto-runs the installer. The hint reads "To update, run the following in PowerShell when entire is not running:" because `irm | iex` does not paste into cmd.exe. The checkpoint-policy call sites that also consume `UpdateCommandForCurrentBinary` share a cross-platform message with no room for the shell hint; they print the command as-is.

## Install detection

Detection is split into per-OS probe files (brew and mise on unix; Scoop and mise on Windows), so the runtime GOOS switch is gone and every OS has an update command. Scoop and mise honor relocated install roots (`SCOOP`, `SCOOP_GLOBAL`, Scoop's `config.json` `root_path`/`global_path`, `MISE_INSTALLS_DIR`, `MISE_DATA_DIR`). Path comparison is case-insensitive on Windows via the shared normalizer. The installer runner is per-OS too; the Windows stub deliberately does not shell through cmd.exe because the PowerShell one-liners would be split on `|` and `&`.

## Known limitation

A user who installed with a custom `-InstallDir` gets the default one-liner and so ends up with a second copy in `%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin`. The installer's PATH-conflict report detects this, names both paths, and on a machine-PATH conflict prints the `-InstallDir <that dir>` remedy. That is a loud warning with an actionable fix, which is better than today's zip from the releases page.

Here is my read on the four. One is substantive, two are cheap and worth doing, one I would dismiss.

**1. Medium: the fallback hint can deliver a parallel Scoop install.** Verified against install.ps1 at line 609. On stable, the script installs through Scoop whenever `scoop` is on PATH and ignores `-InstallDir` on that branch. So a user with a hand-placed `entire.exe` who also has Scoop for other tools runs our hint and ends up with a second entire under `scoop\apps`, while the old one keeps winning on PATH. The installer's conflict warning tells them, but the hint promised an update and delivered a sibling.

The proposed fix is sound but spans two PRs. The `-InstallDir`-opts-out-of-Scoop gate lives in install.ps1, which is #2152's file. Our half, printing `-InstallDir "<dir of entire.exe>"`, is useless until that gate exists, since the script drops the flag today. My recommendation: address it, but sequenced. Add the gate to #2152 or a small follow-up on it, then land the CLI half here once the base has it. If you would rather not grow #2152, leave this open and keep the PR-body limitation note, which already describes exactly this case. Dismissing it is not right, since the report is accurate.

One question the finding raises that is yours to answer: should the README one-liner also get the opt-out, or only the CLI-printed one? I would keep the README Scoop-first. A fresh install has no existing directory to protect, and the CLI hint is the only place we know where the binary lives.

**2. Low: guard order in `scoopAppName`.** The `root != ""` check sits after the `CutPrefix`, so an empty root matches and is then rejected. Correct but reads backwards. Address, it is a two-line reorder.

**3. Low: the Windows auto-update test uses a POSIX mise path.** Fair. The mise row passes a `/home/user/...` path on Windows, so it never exercises backslash conversion or case folding for the mise marker, and the command table has no mise row at all. Address by adding a realistic `C:\Users\test\AppData\Local\mise\installs\...` path.

**4. Low: a test that reads README.md to pin the one-liners.** Dismiss. The drift it guarded against is already fixed, both now say `entire.io/install.ps1` and that URL is no longer branch-bound. A package test reaching four directories up for the README couples the test to repo layout for a string that changes once a year. If the two drift again, the fix is one edit, not a guard.

The editor flagged an undefined constant in the Windows test, but that is a stale view: the constant lives in the Windows-tagged test file and `GOOS=windows` vet, lint, and the tests all pass.

Now finding 1, the Scoop-first parallel install. Where I land:

**The report is right, and the fix has two halves in two repos' worth of ownership.** The gate, "an explicit `-InstallDir` opts out of Scoop", belongs in install.ps1, which is #2152's file. Our half, appending `-InstallDir "<dir of the running exe>"` to the printed one-liner, only helps once that gate exists. Today the script silently drops the flag on the Scoop branch, so shipping our half first prints a flag that does nothing.

**Three ways to sequence it:**

1. **Gate in #2152, CLI half here, land in order.** Cleanest end state. It grows #2152 by roughly ten lines of PowerShell plus a Pester case and a usage-text update, and this PR gains a `-InstallDir` argument in both one-liner constants. The nightly form already uses the scriptblock shape, so stable would switch to it too and both commands get longer.
2. **Both halves in a third stacked PR on top of this one.** Keeps #2152 and #2217 as they are. Costs one more PR in the stack and a reviewer reading three.
3. **Leave it open, ship as is.** The PR body already names this exact case as a known limitation and the installer's conflict report gives the user the `-InstallDir` remedy. It is a loud, actionable warning rather than a silent wrong result.

**My recommendation is 3 for now, then 2 as a follow-up.** The affected population is Windows users who hand-placed the binary and also have Scoop installed. Everything else in this PR is a strict improvement over the releases-page zip, and holding it for a cross-PR change to the installer's Scoop policy blocks that. A follow-up PR can add the gate and the flag together, tested end to end, without either of the current PRs waiting.

**Two things you should decide, not me:**

- Does an explicit `-InstallDir` opting out of Scoop match how you want install.ps1 to behave for README users too? The finding suggests keeping README Scoop-first and only the CLI hint opting out. I agree, since a fresh install has no directory to protect, but it is a policy split worth stating in the script's usage text.
- Should the printed `-InstallDir` be the running exe's directory in all unknown-location cases, including a zip unpacked somewhere odd like `C:\Program Files\Entire`? That is where the user put it, so I would say yes, but writing into Program Files may need elevation the one-liner does not have.

Nothing is missing today. The script does what it was designed to do. The finding argues the design produces the wrong result for one specific user, and proposes a small change.

Here is the exact behavior, at `scripts/install.ps1:608-611`:

```powershell
$scoopCommand = Get-Command "scoop" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
if ($Channel -eq "stable" -and $null -ne $scoopCommand) {
    # Scoop owns the install location and the shims directory it puts on
    # PATH, so -InstallDir and -NoPathUpdate do not apply on this branch.
    Install-EntireWithScoop
```

So on stable, if `scoop` exists on the machine, the script installs through Scoop and ignores `-InstallDir` entirely. That is documented in the usage text and is intentional for a fresh install.

The problem is who runs our printed hint. It goes to a user whose `entire.exe` is at an unknown location, say `C:\Users\me\.local\bin`. If that user also has Scoop for other tools, the hint installs a second entire under `scoop\apps`, and their old binary stays first on PATH at the old version. They asked for an update and got a sibling.

The proposed change is one condition on that `if`: skip the Scoop branch when the caller passed `-InstallDir` explicitly.

```powershell
$explicitDir = $PSBoundParameters.ContainsKey("InstallDir")
if ($Channel -eq "stable" -and $null -ne $scoopCommand -and -not $explicitDir) {
```

Then the CLI hint becomes `... install.ps1 ... -InstallDir "C:\Users\me\.local\bin"`, the script honors it, and the binary is replaced in place. README users who type the bare one-liner still get Scoop-first, because they pass no `-InstallDir`.

That is the whole gap: today there is no way to tell install.ps1 "put it here even though Scoop exists". Without that, appending `-InstallDir` to our hint does nothing on machines with Scoop, which is exactly the machines where the problem occurs.

Too picky for the CLI, but it points at a real message problem in the installer.

**What it asks.** When the binary lives under Program Files, the hint names that directory, and a non-elevated PowerShell will fail writing there. Should the hint add "as Administrator"?

**Why I would dismiss it here.** The CLI would have to guess which directories are machine-owned, which means a heuristic over `ProgramFiles`, `ProgramFiles(x86)`, `ProgramData`, `Windows`, and whatever an admin chose. Anyone who put `entire.exe` under Program Files did so with elevation and knows the drill. Guessing wrong in either direction is worse than saying nothing, and the population is people who hand-unzipped into a system directory.

**What is actually wrong, and it is not in our code.** I checked what install.ps1 does in that case. The rename-aside step at `scripts/install.ps1:352-355` catches any failure from moving the existing exe and reports:

```
Cannot replace <path> because another program holds it open. Close entire ...
```

An access-denied failure lands in the same catch, so a non-elevated user under Program Files is told to close a program that is not running. That is the thing to fix, at the point where the error occurs: distinguish `UnauthorizedAccessException` and say "access denied; run PowerShell as Administrator or pass -InstallDir with a directory you can write to". That is #2152's file and the installer session's territory.

**My recommendation.** Dismiss the finding on this trail with that reasoning, and send the misattributed-error note to the installer session as a small follow-up on #2152. Say the word and I will do both.
